what: ExlService runs data and analytics operations for other companies, and performs the back-office work that sits around them. It builds models and reporting for insurers, healthcare payers and banks, and also processes their claims, underwriting support and customer operations from delivery centres in India and elsewhere.
customers: Insurance companies, healthcare payers and providers, banks and utilities. Contracts usually run several years and are measured in people deployed and processes managed.
money: Claims, underwriting support and actuarial analytics for property-casualty and life insurers.
Payment integrity, risk adjustment and care analytics for health plans.
Data engineering, modelling and AI-enabled services across banking, utilities and retail.
moat: Domain knowledge is the moat here, narrow but real. Insurance claims and healthcare payment integrity have rules that take years to learn, and ExL’s models are trained on the specific data of those industries. Once it runs a payer’s payment integrity process, the institutional knowledge of that client’s edge cases lives inside ExL rather than at the client, which makes the relationship hard to unwind.
risks: Generative AI is a direct threat to the labour-arbitrage half of this business: work that needed a person in a delivery centre may not need one for much longer.
Clients increasingly expect the productivity gains from automation to be passed back as lower prices, which caps revenue growth even where volumes rise.
The shares trade at about 25 times earnings, which is a full price for a services business facing that question.
Revenue is concentrated in insurance and healthcare, so a slowdown in either affects more than half the company.
Debt of $403.6M roughly matches $328.4M of cash, which is manageable but leaves less room for large acquisitions.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $1.1B in 2021 to $2.1B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $2.3B, which is a better record than most peers.
The analytics and data engineering businesses, now the largest segment, earn higher margins than traditional process outsourcing and are less exposed to headcount economics.
Clients who want AI applied to insurance claims or healthcare payments still need someone who understands those processes, which is exactly what ExL sells.
Free cash flow of $271.2M on $2.3B of revenue is a solid conversion rate for a people business.
Eight analysts average a $48.63 target, about 18% above the current price.
watch: Revenue per employee. It is the one number that shows whether ExL captures the benefit of automation or hands it to clients, and it determines whether AI is this company’s opportunity or its problem.
view: Every business process outsourcing company is now priced off a single question, and it is not about their clients or their margins: it is whether generative AI destroys the thing they sell. The traditional model is labour arbitrage — do in Pune for a quarter of the price what a client would do in New Jersey — and if software can do the task for a fiftieth of the price, the arbitrage is worthless. That is why these stocks trade where they do, and any analysis that does not start there is avoiding the point.

ExlService has a better answer than most, and it is worth stating precisely. The company has deliberately shifted its weight from process execution toward analytics and data engineering, which is now its largest segment. In insurance claims and healthcare payment integrity it is not selling hands; it is selling models trained on industry-specific data plus the accumulated knowledge of which edge cases matter for a particular payer. An AI system is only as good as the data and domain rules it is pointed at, and ExL holds both. That is a position from which automation is an opportunity: the same client problem, solved with fewer people and better margins.

The counter-argument is the one I would take seriously. Clients are not naive. When a vendor’s costs fall because software replaced people, procurement departments expect the saving, and contracts in this industry are routinely renegotiated with exactly that logic. The result can be flat revenue on rising volumes and improving internal productivity — all the work of transformation, none of the reward. This is why revenue per employee is the only metric that settles the argument. If it rises materially over the next few years, ExL is capturing the gain. If it is flat while headcount falls, the clients are.

At 25 times earnings you are paying a full price for the optimistic reading. The track record supports some of that — revenue has doubled in four years, which is better than Genpact or WNS managed, and the domain concentration in insurance and healthcare is the right place to be concentrated. But 25 times is not a price at which the AI question can be answered wrongly. I would rather own this at a mid-teens multiple, or own it here in smaller size while watching the one number that matters. The eight analysts at $48.63 are modelling a smooth transition; smooth is not how these transitions usually go.
bull: Domain-specific analytics means ExL applies AI to its clients’ processes and keeps the productivity gain, so revenue per employee rises and margins expand on a growing base.
bear: Clients capture the automation benefit through price renegotiation, revenue flattens as headcount falls, and a 25 times multiple on a labour-arbitrage business unwinds.
